reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / Gorlin's Syndromes of the Head and Neck
clinicalPearls: A non-lethal multiple pterygium syndrome characterised by webbing (pterygia) across the neck, axillae, elbows, knees and fingers
Joint contractures, particularly flexion contractures crossed by the pterygia, limit movement, alongside talipes and camptodactyly
Progressive scoliosis and vertebral anomalies are common and require orthopaedic surveillance
Caused by autosomal recessive variants in CHRNG, encoding the gamma subunit of the foetal acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction
Because the foetal (gamma) receptor is replaced by the adult receptor after birth, the neuromuscular defect is largely limited to the prenatal period, so the condition is non-progressive postnatally
Facial features may include ptosis, downslanting palpebral fissures, a small mouth and micrognathia
Management is supportive with physiotherapy, splinting and surgical release, noting that pterygia often contain neurovascular structures that complicate surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Escobar syndrome is caused by loss-of-function variants in CHRNG, the gene for the gamma subunit of the acetylcholine receptor. This subunit is part of the foetal-type receptor that mediates neuromuscular transmission before birth, when it is normally replaced by the adult epsilon subunit. Deficient foetal neuromuscular transmission reduces foetal movement during development, producing joint contractures and the skin webs (pterygia) that bridge the flexed joints. Because the adult receptor takes over after birth, there is no ongoing myasthenic weakness, and the phenotype is essentially static, distinguishing the Escobar variant from the lethal form.
additionalDifferentials: Klippel-Feil syndrome when neck webbing and vertebral fusion predominate
Noonan or Turner syndrome when neck webbing is isolated
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination mapping the distribution of pterygia and contractures
Molecular genetic testing for CHRNG and a multiple pterygium/neuromuscular junction panel
Spinal radiographs and monitoring for scoliosis and vertebral anomalies
Radiographs of affected limbs to plan surgery
Prenatal ultrasound in at-risk pregnancies for contractures and webbing
Respiratory and feeding assessment where facial or thoracic involvement is present
redFlags: Rapidly progressive scoliosis compromising respiratory function
Neurovascular injury risk during pterygium release surgery
Restrictive lung disease from thoracic and spinal deformity
Feeding or airway difficulty in infants with facial involvement
reference.prognosis: Lifespan is usually normal and intellect is typically preserved; however affected individuals face significant orthopaedic morbidity from contractures and progressive scoliosis, and surgical correction of pterygia is challenging because of contained neurovascular bundles.
pitfalls: Confusing the non-lethal Escobar variant with the lethal multiple pterygium syndrome
Operating on pterygia without recognising that they may contain nerves and vessels
Missing the autosomal recessive inheritance and its recurrence implications
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
Gorlin's Syndromes of the Head and Neck
